title: The Charcoal-Burner and the Fuller
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: There was once a Charcoal-burner who lived and worked by himself. A Fuller, however, happened to come and settle in the same neighbourhood; and the Charcoal-burner, having made his acquaintance and finding he was an agreeable sort of fellow, asked him if he would come and share his house: "We shall get to know one another better that way," he said, "and, beside, our household expenses will be diminished." The Fuller thanked him, but replied, "I couldn't think of it, sir: why, everything I take such pains to whiten would be blackened in no time by your charcoal."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Charcoal-burner live before the Fuller arrives?
options: With several other workers
With his large family
By himself
In the center of a busy town

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fuller do that brings the two men together?
options: He comes and settles in the same neighbourhood
He asks the Charcoal-burner for work
He buys charcoal from him regularly
He builds his house right next door by accident

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Charcoal-burner ask the Fuller to do?
options: Teach him how to whiten cloth
Trade some charcoal for cloth
Move to a different neighbourhood
Come and share his house

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what two reasons does the Charcoal-burner give for sharing a house?
options: They would work faster, and earn more money
They would know each other better, and expenses would be lower
They would be safer, and warmer in winter
They would attract more customers, and sell more goods

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fuller say would happen to his work if he agreed?
options: He would have no room left to work
He would have to pay for his own charcoal
Everything he whitens would be blackened by the charcoal
He would lose his customers to the Charcoal-burner

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Fuller respond to the invitation overall?
options: He thanks the Charcoal-burner but declines
He accepts at once, delighted by the offer
He asks for time to think it over
He suggests sharing a house with someone else instead

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Charcoal-burner think sharing a house is a good idea?
options: He has run out of money to live alone any longer
He wants the Fuller to teach him a new trade
He plans to give up charcoal-burning for good
He values the Fuller's company and the savings it would bring, without considering their trades conflict

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why is the Fuller's trade fundamentally incompatible with the Charcoal-burner's?
options: The two men need completely different tools that cannot be stored together
One trade's work relies on making things white, and the other's leaves soot and black dust everywhere
The two trades require working at opposite times of day
The two men would compete for the same customers

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "diminished" mean in "our household expenses will be diminished"?
options: Increased
Recorded
Reduced
Shared equally

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Friendship alone is not enough reason to combine two incompatible trades
Living alone is always better than sharing a home
Charcoal-burners and Fullers should never live in the same town
Saving money is more important than any other concern

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Charcoal-burner think of the Fuller once he meets him?
options: That he is too proud to be a good neighbor
That he talks too much about his own trade
That he seems untrustworthy at first
That he is an agreeable sort of fellow

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what trade does a Fuller practice, based on how he describes his own work?
options: Burning charcoal
Whitening cloth
Selling firewood
Dyeing wool black

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Fuller address the Charcoal-burner when declining?
options: "Friend"
"Neighbor"
"Sir"
"Stranger"

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Fuller phrase his refusal so firmly, saying he "couldn't think of it"?
options: He recognizes the arrangement would ruin his work no matter how friendly they are
He does not actually like the Charcoal-burner very much
He has already agreed to live somewhere else
He believes the Charcoal-burner cannot afford to share expenses

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the phrase "in no time" suggest about how quickly the Fuller's work would be ruined?
options: Only after many months
Gradually, over several years
Only during certain seasons
Very quickly, almost immediately

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "acquaintance" mean in "having made his acquaintance"?
options: A close and lifelong friend
A person one has come to know a little
A business partner with a signed contract
A rival competing for the same customers

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Charcoal-burner refuses to let the Fuller move into the neighbourhood
Two men successfully share a house and split their expenses
A Fuller politely refuses to share a house because the two trades would ruin each other
A Fuller teaches the Charcoal-burner how to whiten cloth
